weaknesses: The method is not specified sufficiently for reproduction. Evidence for the central mechanisms is weak. “Context collapse” is demonstrated with one Dynamic Cheatsheet trajectory, without its frequency across runs or a controlled length-matched comparison. The empirical scope and statistical rigor are insufficient for the broad claims: all experiments use one base model, only three datasets from two application areas are tested, no repeated runs or confidence intervals are reported, and online results use only one shuffled test order. FiNER performance without reliable labels actually falls below the base model.

The online protocol raises a comparability concern. ACE updates on the test stream and its AppWorld Reflector prompt consumes unit-test reports, which are close to evaluator feedback even when reference code is withheld. The paper must clarify exactly what feedback is available, demonstrate that hidden evaluation information is not leaked, and avoid directly equating this protocol with static pass@1 leaderboard systems.

Baseline and efficiency comparisons are not adequately controlled. Several claims are reported inconsistently or too strongly. Claims that longer contexts need not increase serving cost are also unsupported by measurements.

The novelty over Dynamic Cheatsheet and related structured agent-memory systems appears primarily combinatorial, yet direct comparisons and mechanism-specific ablations are missing.
